questions.q: A student observes two cells under a microscope: Cell A has a distinct nuclear membrane and 80S ribosomes; Cell B lacks a nuclear membrane and has 70S ribosomes. Which cell is prokaryotic and which is eukaryotic? Justify your answer using two structural criteria.
questions.a: Cell A is eukaryotic (presence of nuclear membrane and 80S ribosomes); Cell B is prokaryotic (absence of nuclear membrane and presence of 70S ribosomes). A wrong answer reveals the student cannot distinguish the defining feature - the nuclear envelope - or confuses ribosome sedimentation coefficients, indicating they memorized labels without understanding the structural basis of the prokaryotic-eukaryotic divide.

questions.q: Why do prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum, yet still carry out aerobic respiration and protein synthesis? Explain the structural adaptation that allows this.
questions.a: Prokaryotes perform aerobic respiration using enzymes embedded in their plasma membrane (mesosomes increase surface area) and synthesize proteins on free-floating 70S ribosomes in the cytoplasm. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks prokaryotes cannot perform these functions, or that they possess primitive versions of eukaryotic organelles, revealing a misconception that membrane-bound organelles are absolutely required for these processes rather than being eukaryotic specializations for compartmentalization.

questions.q: A researcher discovers a new single-celled organism in a hot spring. It has a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, circular DNA not enclosed by a membrane, 70S ribosomes, and divides by binary fission. However, it also has histone-like proteins associated with its DNA. Classify this organism and explain whether the histone-like proteins make it eukaryotic.
questions.a: The organism is prokaryotic (bacteria/archaea). Histone-like proteins in archaea and some bacteria organize DNA but do not form a true nucleus with a nuclear envelope. A wrong classification as eukaryotic reveals the student equates any DNA-protein association with eukaryotic chromatin, missing the critical distinction: eukaryotes have histone octamers forming nucleosomes within a membrane-bound nucleus, while prokaryotes have nucleoid-associated proteins without membrane enclosure.

questions.q: Compare the cell envelope of Gram-positive bacteria, Gram-negative bacteria, and a typical plant cell. Analyze how the structural differences in their outermost layers relate to their staining properties and mechanical strength.
questions.a: Gram-positive bacteria have thick peptidoglycan with teichoic acids (retains crystal violet); Gram-negative have thin peptidoglycan plus outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (loses crystal violet, takes safranin); plant cells have cellulose-hemicellulose-pectin cell wall outside plasma membrane (no Gram staining). A poor analysis shows the student cannot link chemical composition to staining outcome or confuses bacterial cell envelope layers with eukaryotic cell wall composition, indicating surface-level memorization without structural reasoning.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Since mitochondrial and chloroplast ribosomes are 70S like prokaryotic ribosomes, mitochondria and chloroplasts must be prokaryotic cells living inside eukaryotic cells." Is this reasoning valid? Justify using endosymbiotic theory evidence.
questions.a: The reasoning is partially valid but incomplete. The 70S ribosomes, circular DNA, and double membranes support endosymbiotic origin, but mitochondria/chloroplasts are NOT independent prokaryotic cells - they have lost most genes to the nuclear genome, cannot survive independently, and their protein synthesis depends on nuclear-encoded proteins. A student agreeing fully reveals they confuse "prokaryotic-like features" with "being a prokaryote," missing the evolutionary transition from endosymbiont to organelle.

questions.q: Design a simple microscopy-based experiment to distinguish between a culture of cyanobacteria (prokaryotic) and Chlamydomonas (eukaryotic green alga) without using stains. Specify what you would observe and how each observation confirms the cell type.
questions.a: Use phase-contrast microscopy: cyanobacteria will show no distinct nucleus, uniform cytoplasm with thylakoid membranes (no chloroplasts), and possible heterocysts; Chlamydomonas will show a clear nucleus, cup-shaped chloroplast with pyrenoid, two anterior flagella, and contractile vacuoles. A poor design might suggest Gram staining (both are Gram-negative) or size alone (overlap exists), revealing the student doesn't know which structures are visibly distinct in unstained live cells.
